selected_passages.title: sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line
selected_passages.text: Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

Helena World Chronicle, LLC has filed a class action antitrust lawsuit against Google and Alphabet in the U.S. District Court in D.C., alleging that Google's AI technologies, including Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard, along with older features like the Knowledge Graph, are siphoning content, readers, and ad revenue from news publishers. The suit claims these practices violate the Sherman Act and Clayton Act by discouraging users from visiting publisher websites, potentially causing publishers to lose 20-40% of their traffic, and seeks an injunction requiring consent for using publisher data to train AI models.

selected_passages.text:
- The trial is titled US v. Google.
- Eddy Cue is a witness for Apple.
- Judge Amit Mehta presided over the case.

- Google CEO Sundar Pichai was involved in the 2016 renegotiation.

- Three iPhone screenshots were shown regarding setup process.
- Screenshots included the Appearance screen, location-tracking prompt, and App Tracking Transparency pop-up.
- DuckDuckGo's CEO testified previously claiming switching search engines takes too many steps.
- Safari was introduced in early 2003.
- Before 2003, users had to manually type google.com to search.
- Apple deals with Yahoo and Bing to make those services easy to find.
- The ISA represents a significant portion of Apple's profits.
- Specific revenue numbers were discussed in closed court sessions.
- Google pays Apple billions of dollars a year.
- Apple believes it has better privacy than Google.
- The ISA requires Google to allow searching without logging in.
- Apple makes it harder for Google to track users via Safari.
- The courtroom had a monitor malfunction during testimony.
- Judge Mehta joked about Apple making a donation if they wanted to switch.
- Cue stated Apple would never consider walking away from the deal if revenue share couldn't be agreed upon.
- Cue claimed he couldn't remember the names of some search engine alternatives.

selected_passages.text:
- Eddy Cue testified that there was no valid alternative to Google Search for Apple devices at the time of the deal.
- The Information Services Agreement (ISA) makes Google the default search engine on Apple products in exchange for billions in payments.
- Apple believes in protecting user privacy but also maintains a strong partnership with Google, creating a central tension in the trial.
- Cue argued that showing users alternative search engines during setup would degrade the user experience and slow down device onboarding.
- The Justice Department questions whether Apple's choice of Google is based on product quality or financial incentives.

selected_passages.title: raw:sources/News_publisher_files_class_action_antitrust_suit_against_Google_citing_AI_s_harms_to_their_bottom_line
selected_passages.text: A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.

The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.
